Small businesses are often described as the backbone of a nation's economy. Though each one may seem modest on its own, together they generate a remarkable share of employment and output. In many countries, firms with fewer than fifty workers account for more than half of all private-sector jobs. One of the greatest contributions of small businesses is their ability to create employment quickly. Because they require relatively little capital to start, they can spring up in towns and villages where large corporations rarely venture. This helps distribute economic opportunity more evenly across a country. Small enterprises are also engines of innovation. Free from the rigid hierarchies of giant companies, they can experiment boldly with new products and ideas. Many technologies that we now take for granted began in tiny workshops run by a handful of determined individuals. However, small businesses face formidable obstacles. Access to affordable credit remains a persistent difficulty, and a single bad season can push an owner toward bankruptcy. Complicated regulations and delayed payments further hamper their growth, discouraging many would-be entrepreneurs. For these reasons, governments that wish to strengthen their economies must nurture small businesses deliberately. Simplifying rules, offering easy loans and providing training can transform struggling ventures into thriving ones. In doing so, a nation invests not merely in commerce but in the prosperity of its people.
